ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

When routine testing is unnecessary

A well-appearing 18-month-old has a typical barking cough, hoarseness and mild stridor only when upset after a viral prodrome. There is no drooling, focal chest finding or choking history. Which diagnostic approach is most appropriate?

  1. Clinical diagnosis without routine laboratory testing or imaging
  2. Lateral neck radiography before giving a corticosteroid
  3. Routine viral PCR to select a croup-specific antiviral
  4. Blood culture and inflammatory markers for every episode
  5. Bronchoscopy to exclude a congenital narrowing at the first typical episode
Answer and explanation

Clinical diagnosis without routine laboratory testing or imaging

Typical uncomplicated croup is a clinical diagnosis; unnecessary procedures can distress the child without changing care.

Option explanations

Clinical diagnosis without routine laboratory testing or imaging: Typical uncomplicated croup is a clinical diagnosis; unnecessary procedures can distress the child without changing care.

Lateral neck radiography before giving a corticosteroid: A typical uncomplicated presentation does not require radiographic confirmation before treatment.

Routine viral PCR to select a croup-specific antiviral: Routine viral identification generally does not guide treatment of typical croup.

Blood culture and inflammatory markers for every episode: These are not routinely indicated in a well-appearing child with a typical presentation.

Bronchoscopy to exclude a congenital narrowing at the first typical episode: Airway endoscopy is reserved for selected atypical or recurrent patterns rather than routine typical croup.
